event_name: Islamic New Year — Ras al-Sanah al-Hijriyyah
short_description: The first day of Muharram marks the beginning of the Islamic Hijri lunar calendar, formally established by Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (ra) in 17 AH, anchored to the Prophet's migration (Hijra) to Madinah as year one.
importance: An occasion for personal reflection, gratitude, and renewal of intentions (niyyah) for the year ahead. Muharram itself is a sacred month, and its arrival is a reminder of the blessings of time.
authenticity_note: The Hijri calendar established by Umar (ra) is well-documented in historical sources. No specific acts of worship are prescribed for this day by authentic hadith; any elaborate celebration of the new year is an innovation (bid'ah).

short_description: The Prophet ﷺ found the Jews of Madinah fasting this day, commemorating Allah saving Musa (as) and Banu Isra'il from Pharaoh. He fasted it, commanded Muslims to fast, and intended to also fast the 9th to distinguish from Jewish practice.
importance: Fasting Ashura expiates the sins of the previous year (Muslim). The recommended practice is to fast the 9th and 10th together. One of the most emphasized voluntary fasts in Islam.
authenticity_note: Firmly established in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. The martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali (ra) at Karbala also occurred on this day in 61 AH; public mourning rituals are not from the authentic Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.

event_name: Month of Safar — Rejection of Superstitions
short_description: Pre-Islamic Arabs considered Safar an unlucky month. The Prophet ﷺ explicitly rejected all such superstitions, affirming there are no inherently cursed days, months, or omens in Islam.
importance: Reminds Muslims to reject tiyarah (superstition) and maintain complete tawakkul in Allah. 'There is no adwa, no tiyarah, no hama, and no Safar.' (Bukhari, Muslim)
authenticity_note: The hadith negating bad omens tied to Safar is sahih, reported in Bukhari and Muslim. No specific act of worship is prescribed for this month; any ritual designated for Safar lacks authentic basis.

event_name: Beginning of the Prophet's ﷺ Final Illness
short_description: Toward the end of Safar 11 AH, the Prophet ﷺ began to experience the illness that would lead to his passing. He continued to lead prayers and deliver guidance throughout this period until he could no longer do so.
importance: The final weeks of the Prophet's life were filled with profound farewell guidance and reminders to protect the Sunnah and maintain unity — a period of deep reflection for all Muslims.
authenticity_note: The onset in late Safar 11 AH is recorded in seerah literature (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham). The precise day is not confirmed by hadith; late Safar 11 AH is a general scholarly estimate.

event_name: Birth of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — Mawlid al-Nabi
short_description: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant (approximately 570 CE) in Makkah. He is the final messenger of Allah, sent as a mercy to all of creation.
importance: 'And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.' (Quran 21:107). His birth represents the arrival of the final guidance for all of humanity until the Day of Judgment.
authenticity_note: The Year of the Elephant is widely agreed upon. The exact date is disputed: 12 Rabi al-Awwal is most commonly cited (Ibn Ishaq), but 9 Rabi al-Awwal is preferred by some researchers. Whether to formally celebrate Mawlid is a scholarly difference (khilaf); neither position is unanimous.

short_description: The Prophet ﷺ passed away on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, 11 AH (June 8, 632 CE), in the home of Aisha (ra) in Madinah, at approximately 63 years of age, marking the end of prophethood.
importance: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger. Other messengers have passed on before him...' (Quran 3:144). A day for profound reflection on following his Sunnah and preserving his legacy.
authenticity_note: 12 Rabi al-Awwal 11 AH is the most widely accepted date among scholars and historians, including Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Sa'd. This date coincides with the most commonly reported birth date.

event_name: Hijra — Prophet ﷺ Arrives in Madinah
short_description: After migrating from Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ stopped at Quba on 8 Rabi al-Awwal — founding the first mosque in Islam — then entered Madinah on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, 1 AH, completing the historic migration.
importance: The Hijra marks the birth of the Muslim community as a unified entity. Umar (ra) designated it as the start of the Islamic calendar. 'Indeed, those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the cause of Allah...' (Quran 8:72)
authenticity_note: Arrival in Madinah in Rabi al-Awwal 1 AH is well-documented. Most sources cite arrival at Quba on 8 Rabi al-Awwal and entry into Madinah on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, though some variation exists in early historical accounts.

short_description: Upon arriving in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ purchased a plot of land and built Masjid al-Nabawi with the Companions in Rabi al-Awwal 1 AH. It became the center of Islamic worship, governance, education, and community life.
importance: Prayer in Masjid al-Nabawi carries a reward of 1,000 prayers (Ibn Majah, Sahih). It is the second most sacred mosque in Islam and contains the grave of the Prophet ﷺ.
authenticity_note: Founded in Rabi al-Awwal 1 AH is established in historical sources. The precise day is not confirmed; it was built shortly after the Prophet's arrival. The reward multiplier is from authentic hadith.

short_description: The fourth month of the Islamic calendar. No specific major religious event is universally designated for this month by authentic narrations.
importance: A time for continued worship, following the Sunnah, and maintaining spiritual consistency through regular salah, dhikr, and voluntary good deeds.
authenticity_note: No events of major religious significance are authenticated for this month with firm, precise dates. Some historical events occurred during this month but their exact days are not confirmed.

short_description: The first engagement between Muslims and the Byzantine Empire, fought in 8 AH near modern-day Jordan. Three commanders — Zayd ibn Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawaha — were successively martyred. Khalid ibn al-Walid (ra) then led a brilliant tactical withdrawal.
importance: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (ra) earned the title 'Dhu al-Janahayn' (one with two wings in Paradise). The battle showcased Companion bravery and Khalid's genius, who became 'the Sword of Allah.'
authenticity_note: Well-documented in authentic hadith and seerah literature. Occurred in Jumada al-Ula 8 AH; the precise day within the month is not firmly established.

short_description: The sixth month of the Islamic calendar. The death of Fatimah al-Zahra (ra), daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, is placed by some scholars in this month in 11 AH, though dates vary significantly among historical sources.
importance: An opportunity for consistent worship, generosity, and maintaining one's connection to Allah through the regular acts of the Sunnah.
authenticity_note: The death of Fatimah (ra) is disputed — some scholars say 3 months after the Prophet's death, others say 6 or 8 months. No single date commands scholarly consensus. No major obligatory observances are designated for this month.

event_name: Month of Rajab Begins — One of the Four Sacred Months
short_description: Rajab is one of the four sacred months (al-Ashhur al-Hurum). It is a time for increased dhikr, istighfar, and voluntary worship, and was historically a month of ceasefire enabling free movement for pilgrimage and trade.
importance: 'Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve... of these, four are sacred.' (Quran 9:36). Sinning in sacred months carries greater weight; good deeds are especially encouraged.
authenticity_note: Rajab as a sacred month is established in Quran (9:36) and authentic Sunnah. Special prayers designated specifically for Rajab (e.g., Salat al-Raghaib) and specific fasts beyond general voluntary fasting lack strong hadith support.

event_name: Laylat al-Isra wal-Mi'raj — Night Journey and Ascension
short_description: The miraculous night on which Allah transported the Prophet ﷺ from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa (Isra), then ascended him through the seven heavens (Mi'raj), where the five daily prayers were made obligatory on the Muslim ummah.
importance: One of the greatest miracles of the Prophet ﷺ. The five daily Salah were ordained on this night. 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa...' (Quran 17:1)
authenticity_note: The event is affirmed in Quran (17:1, 53:1-18) and authentic hadith (Bukhari, Muslim). The exact date is disputed. 27 Rajab is the most popular but not confirmed by scholarly consensus; other opinions include Rabi al-Awwal and Ramadan. Imam al-Nawawi noted the date cannot be determined with certainty. Display as approximate on your calendar.

short_description: In Rajab 9 AH, the Prophet ﷺ led the largest Muslim army (30,000 men) to Tabuk in response to news of a Byzantine military buildup. The march took place in extreme heat during harvest season. No battle occurred; the Byzantines withdrew and the Prophet returned after 20 days.
importance: Surah al-Tawbah extensively addresses this expedition — the hypocrites who stayed behind, and the three honest Companions who missed it and were later forgiven. A supreme test of sincere faith over personal comfort.
authenticity_note: Rajab 9 AH is established in seerah literature. Covered extensively in Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and the major seerah works. The exact day of departure is not precisely confirmed.

event_name: Month of Sha'ban — Sunnah of Increased Fasting
short_description: The Prophet ﷺ used to fast more in Sha'ban than in any other month outside Ramadan. He explained it is a month people neglect, between Rajab and Ramadan, and a month in which deeds are raised to Allah.
importance: 'It is a month in which deeds are raised to the Lord of the Worlds, and I love for my deeds to be raised while I am fasting.' (Nasa'i, Hasan). Spiritual preparation for Ramadan.
authenticity_note: Established in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (narration of Aisha ra). The hadith about deeds being raised in Sha'ban is graded hasan. Fasting is recommended but not obligatory.

short_description: The 15th night of Sha'ban is reported in some narrations as a night of divine mercy and forgiveness, where Allah looks upon His creation and forgives many. Some early scholars recommended increased du'a and personal worship on this night.
importance: If the narrations are accepted, it is a night for sincere istighfar and du'a. No congregational special prayers or mandatory fasting are established by strong hadith.
authenticity_note: A point of scholarly difference. Some supporting hadith are graded da'if by scholars like al-Albani, while others including Ibn Taymiyyah acknowledged some basis for its virtue. Special communal rituals or singling out this day for fasting lack strong support. Treat as having possible but not confirmed virtue in your app.

event_name: Change of Qibla — From Jerusalem to Makkah
short_description: By divine command in Sha'ban 2 AH, the direction of prayer (Qibla) was changed from Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Makkah. The congregation pivoted mid-prayer the moment the verse was revealed.
importance: 'Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.' (Quran 2:144). This established the unique Qibla of the Muslim ummah, distinct from all other communities.
authenticity_note: Well-documented in Sahih al-Bukhari. The month of Sha'ban 2 AH is scholarly consensus. The precise day is not established. The mosque in Madinah where this occurred is Masjid al-Qiblatayn (Mosque of the Two Qiblas).

event_name: Beginning of Ramadan — Month of Fasting
short_description: The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, Ramadan, is the month of obligatory fasting (Sawm) from Fajr to Maghrib. It is the month the Quran was first revealed, and a month of mercy, forgiveness, and liberation from Hellfire.
importance: One of the Five Pillars of Islam. 'The month of Ramadan is that in which was revealed the Quran, a guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and criterion.' (Quran 2:185)
authenticity_note: Firmly established in Quran (2:183-185) and mutawatir Sunnah. Fasting Ramadan is among the most certain obligations in the religion.

short_description: Fought on 17 Ramadan 2 AH. The Muslim army of 313 men faced a Qurayshi force of ~950. Despite being outnumbered and under-armed, Allah granted the Muslims a decisive and miraculous victory — 70 Quraysh were killed and 70 taken captive.
importance: Allah called it 'Yawm al-Furqan' — the Day of Criterion between truth and falsehood (Quran 8:41). This victory established the Muslim community as a formidable force in Arabia.
authenticity_note: 17 Ramadan 2 AH is the widely accepted date in seerah literature (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, al-Waqidi). Confirmed through multiple chains of narration.

short_description: On 20 Ramadan 8 AH, the Prophet ﷺ led 10,000 Muslims into Makkah in a triumphant, nearly bloodless conquest. The Kaaba was purified of 360 idols. The Prophet ﷺ declared a general amnesty: 'Go, for you are free.'
importance: The greatest military and spiritual victory of the early Muslims. Surah al-Fath (48) celebrates this event. It marked the definitive end of organized polytheism in Makkah and opened Arabia to Islam.
authenticity_note: 20 Ramadan 8 AH is the most widely cited and accepted date in seerah sources (Ibn Ishaq, al-Waqidi, Ibn Sa'd, and others).

event_name: Last Ten Nights of Ramadan — I'tikaf and Intensified Worship
short_description: The final ten nights of Ramadan contain Laylat al-Qadr and are the most virtuous nights of the year. The Prophet ﷺ would intensify his worship, wake his family for prayer, and perform I'tikaf (spiritual seclusion in the mosque).
importance: 'Seek Laylat al-Qadr in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan.' (Bukhari, Muslim). I'tikaf during these ten nights is a confirmed, unbroken Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.
authenticity_note: Well-established in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. I'tikaf is sunnah mu'akkadah. The Prophet ﷺ never abandoned it until his death.

hijri_date_display: Odd nights of last 10 — most cited: 27 Ramadan
short_description: The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months of worship (Quran 97:3). On this night the Quran was first revealed, Jibril and the angels descend with every divine decree, and peace reigns until Fajr.
importance: Worship on this single night surpasses 83+ years of continuous worship. The Prophet ﷺ taught a specific du'a: 'Allahumma innaka afuwwun tuhibbu al-afwa fa'fu anni.' (Tirmidhi, Sahih)
authenticity_note: Firmly established in Quran (Surah 97, Surah 44:3) and authentic hadith. The exact night is deliberately concealed by Allah. The 27th is most commonly cited but the Prophet ﷺ commanded seeking it in ALL odd nights of the last ten: 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th, or 29th.

event_name: First Revelation of the Quran — Beginning of Prophethood
short_description: The first verses of the Quran were revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in the Cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur, Makkah, during the last ten nights of Ramadan. Jibril (as) appeared and conveyed Surah al-Alaq 1-5: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created...'
importance: The beginning of Quranic revelation marks the start of the prophetic mission and the arrival of the final, preserved divine guidance for all of humanity until the Day of Judgment.
authenticity_note: Established in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Confirmed in Quran (2:185, 97:1). The exact day is unknown — it occurred in the last ten nights of Ramadan, approximately 13 years before Hijra. Display the general period, not a specific day.

short_description: Hasan ibn Ali (ra), eldest grandson of the Prophet ﷺ and son of Ali and Fatimah (ra), was born in Ramadan 3 AH. The Prophet ﷺ performed adhan in his ear, conducted aqiqah, and named him Hasan.
importance: 'Hasan and Husayn are the leaders of the youth of Paradise.' (Tirmidhi, Sahih). He is among the most beloved figures in Islamic history.
authenticity_note: Birth in Ramadan 3 AH is mentioned in historical sources. The precise day within Ramadan has variation among scholars; the hadith about his status in Paradise is sahih.

event_name: Eid al-Fitr — Festival of Breaking the Fast
short_description: The first day of Shawwal marks Eid al-Fitr, the celebration at the end of Ramadan. Muslims perform the Eid prayer in congregation, pay Zakat al-Fitr before the prayer, and celebrate with family and community.
importance: One of the two divinely ordained festivals. Zakat al-Fitr is wajib (obligatory) before the Eid prayer. 'The fasting person has two occasions of joy: when he breaks his fast, and when he meets his Lord.' (Bukhari, Muslim)
authenticity_note: Firmly established in the Quran and mutawatir Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ designated only two festivals for Muslims: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

short_description: Muslims are encouraged to fast any six days during Shawwal. Combined with Ramadan, this equals fasting the entire year — since each good deed is multiplied tenfold (30 days + 6 days × 10 = 360 days).
importance: 'Whoever fasts Ramadan and then follows it with six days of Shawwal, it will be as if he fasted the entire year.' (Sahih Muslim). A simple yet immensely rewarding Sunnah.
authenticity_note: Established in Sahih Muslim (Hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari). The six fasts may be done consecutively or spread throughout Shawwal; they need not start immediately after Eid.

short_description: Fought in Shawwal 3 AH at the mountain of Uhud near Madinah. Muslims initially gained the upper hand but suffered a severe setback when archers abandoned their posts to collect war spoils, against the Prophet's ﷺ explicit command. Seventy Companions were martyred, including Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib (ra).
importance: Surah Al Imran (3:121-179) extensively addresses Uhud, extracting lessons in obedience to the Prophet ﷺ and the consequences of prioritizing dunya over his command.
authenticity_note: 7 Shawwal 3 AH is the widely accepted date in seerah literature (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham). Well-documented in Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and the major seerah works.

short_description: Fought in Shawwal 8 AH against the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes shortly after the Conquest of Makkah. Despite an initial ambush causing temporary Muslim retreat, Allah sent sakinah (divine tranquility) and the Muslims rallied to win decisively.
importance: 'Allah has already given you victory in many regions and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you but it did not avail you at all...' (Quran 9:25). A profound lesson in reliance on Allah over numbers.
authenticity_note: Shawwal 8 AH is established in seerah sources. The exact day is not precisely confirmed. Well-documented in seerah and tafsir literature.

event_name: Marriage of Prophet ﷺ to Aisha (ra) — Nikah Consummated
short_description: The Prophet ﷺ consummated his marriage to Aisha bint Abi Bakr (ra) in Shawwal 1 AH. Aisha (ra) became the most prolific female transmitter of hadith, conveying the Prophet's private conduct, worship, and rulings.
importance: Aisha (ra) transmitted over 2,210 hadith and was the primary source for understanding the Prophet's ﷺ personal worship and household conduct. She encouraged marriages in Shawwal based on this.
authenticity_note: Shawwal is established as the month of consummation in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Aisha herself. The specific day is not confirmed.

event_name: Month of Dhul Qa'dah Begins — Sacred Month
short_description: Dhul Qa'dah is one of the four sacred months. Historically a month of ceasefire in Arabia, enabling free travel for pilgrimage and trade. Fighting in it was a grave violation of divine and social law.
importance: One of the sacred months mentioned in Quran 9:36. Sinning in these months carries greater weight. A time for restraint, worship, and spiritual preparation before Dhul Hijjah.
authenticity_note: Established in Quran (9:36) and authentic Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ identified the four sacred months in the Farewell Khutbah.

short_description: In Dhul Qa'dah 6 AH, the Prophet ﷺ led ~1,400 Companions toward Makkah for Umrah but was stopped at Hudaybiyyah. A 10-year peace treaty was signed with Quraysh. Though the terms appeared unfavorable, Allah declared it 'a clear victory' (Quran 48:1).
importance: Led to the rapid spread of Islam as the Prophet ﷺ could now freely invite kings and tribes. The following two years saw more people enter Islam than in all preceding years combined. A masterclass in strategic patience and trust in Allah.
authenticity_note: Dhul Qa'dah 6 AH is established in seerah and hadith sources (Bukhari, Muslim, Ibn Ishaq). The precise day within the month is not confirmed.

event_name: Battle of the Trench — Ghazwat al-Khandaq
short_description: A coalition of Arab tribes (~10,000 men) besieged Madinah in Dhul Qa'dah 5 AH. On the advice of Salman al-Farisi (ra), Muslims dug a defensive trench around the vulnerable side of the city. After a 27-day siege, Allah sent wind and divine intervention that scattered the coalition.
importance: Surah al-Ahzab (33:9-27) addresses this event directly. It demonstrates that strategic thinking, patience, and complete tawakkul in Allah are core Islamic virtues. It effectively ended Qurayshi military dominance.
authenticity_note: Dhul Qa'dah 5 AH is the established date according to most seerah scholars (some say Shawwal 5 AH). Well-documented in Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and major seerah works.

event_name: First Ten Days of Dhul Hijjah — Most Virtuous Days of the Year
short_description: The first ten days of Dhul Hijjah are the most virtuous days of the entire year. Fasting (especially the 9th), dhikr (takbir, tahmid, tahlil), Quran recitation, and charity are strongly recommended for all Muslims.
importance: 'There are no days on which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these ten days.' (Sahih al-Bukhari). Ibn Abbas (ra) said the 'ten nights' in Quran (89:2) refer to these very days.
authenticity_note: Firmly established in Sahih al-Bukhari and other authentic collections. The general takbir (Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, La ilaha illallah...) during these days is a confirmed Sunnah of the Companions.

short_description: On the 8th of Dhul Hijjah, Hajj pilgrims enter ihram and move from Makkah to Mina, where they spend the day and night in prayer and remembrance before the standing at Arafat on the 9th.
importance: An essential day of Hajj — one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Non-pilgrims may continue voluntary fasting of the first nine days of Dhul Hijjah.
authenticity_note: Established in authentic Sunnah and agreed upon by all four major madhabs. The name 'Tarwiyah' has several explanations in classical fiqh literature.

short_description: The climax of Hajj. Pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafat from noon to sunset in du'a, dhikr, and repentance. For non-pilgrims, fasting this day expiates two years of sins. The completion of Islam was announced on this day.
importance: 'Hajj is Arafah.' (Tirmidhi, Sahih). 'Today I have perfected your religion for you...' (Quran 5:3, revealed on this day). Fasting Arafah expiates the previous and coming year's sins (Muslim).
authenticity_note: 9 Dhul Hijjah is firmly established in Sahih Muslim and across all authentic sources. Fasting for non-pilgrims is in Sahih Muslim. Fasting on Arafah for pilgrims themselves is makruh (disliked) per the Prophet's ﷺ practice.

event_name: Eid al-Adha — Festival of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr)
short_description: The greatest festival in Islam, commemorating Prophet Ibrahim's (as) willingness to sacrifice his son Ismail (as) in complete submission to Allah. Muslims perform the Eid prayer then sacrifice an animal (udhiyyah) — distributing its meat to family, neighbors, and the poor.
importance: The Prophet ﷺ said Yawm al-Nahr is the greatest day of the year. The udhiyyah is wajib according to the Hanafi school and confirmed Sunnah according to the majority. It commemorates Ibrahim's (as) ultimate tawakkul.
authenticity_note: Firmly established in Quran (22:34-37, 108:2) and mutawatir Sunnah. 10 Dhul Hijjah is unanimously agreed upon by all scholars.

short_description: The three days following Eid al-Adha. Pilgrims remain in Mina and pelt the three jamarat. These are days of celebration, eating, drinking, and intense remembrance of Allah. Fasting on these days is strictly prohibited.
importance: 'The days of Tashriq are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah.' (Muslim). The udhiyyah sacrifice is valid through the 13th. Pilgrims departing before sunset on the 12th may do so (nafr awwal).
authenticity_note: Established in Sahih Muslim and other authentic collections. The prohibition of fasting on Ayyam al-Tashriq is unanimously agreed upon by all major scholars.

short_description: In Dhul Hijjah 10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ performed his only and final Hajj. On Yawm Arafah, he delivered the historic Farewell Sermon (Khutbat al-Wada), affirming the sanctity of Muslim life, property and honor; equality of all people before Allah; and the rights of women.
importance: The verse 'Today I have perfected your religion for you...' (Quran 5:3) was revealed during this Hajj. The Farewell Sermon is the Prophet's ﷺ final comprehensive address to the entire ummah — he asked three times if he had delivered the message.
authenticity_note: Dhul Hijjah 10 AH is firmly established in Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and all major seerah sources. The Farewell Sermon is established through multiple authentic chains (mutawatir in meaning).
